questions.question: Explain the use of FOREIGN KEY constraint in SQL. Write SQL commands to create a STUDENT table with a foreign key referencing DEPARTMENT. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the use of FOREIGN KEY constraint in SQL Write SQL commands to create
  • a STUDENT table with a foreign key referencing DEPARTMENT. [A]/[CO3]
  • The FOREIGN KEY constraint in SQL is used to link two tables and maintain
  • referential integrity between them. It ensures that the value in one table (child) matches
  • a valid value in another table (parent). For example, each student must belong to a valid
  • department.
  • CREATE TABLE DEPARTMENT (
  • DeptID INT PRIMARY KEY ,
  • DeptName V ARCHAR(50)
  • );
  • CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
  • StudentID INT PRIMARY KEY ,
  • StudName V ARCHAR(40),
  • DeptID INT,
  • FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(DeptID)
  • );
  • Explanation of FOREIGN KEY constraint and its usage in SQL - 2.5 marks
  • Example SQL commands- 2.5 marks

questions.question: Explain the concept of a key attribute and describe how it is identified in a database system / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of a key attribute and describe how it is identified in a database
  • system. [U]/[C01]
  • A key attribute is a field or a set of fields in a table that uniquely identifies each record
  • in that table. It helps prevent duplicate entries and ensures accurate data retrieval.
  • In a DBMS, a key attribute is identified by finding an attribute (or a combination of
  • attributes) that can uniquely distinguish each record in a table. It is usually chosen as
  • the Primary Key because it ensures uniqueness and does not allow null values. Database
  • designers analyze data dependencies and relationships between attributes to determine
  • which one can serve as the key.
  • Explanation of key attribute – 3 marks
  • Explanation of how it is identified – 2 marks

questions.question: Describe entities and attributes. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Entities and Attributes. (5 Marks)
  • Scheme
  • Definition of Entity – An entity in DBMS represents a real-world object or concept that can be
  • uniquely identified and stored in a database. It forms the foundation of data modeling in an
  • Entity-Relationship (ER) model.(1)
  • Example: A student, An employee, or bank a/c, etc. all are entities.(1)
  • Types of Entities such as strong,weak,Derived,Multivalued etc.(1)
  • Definition of Attribute – An Attribute is a property or characteristic that describes an entity in a
  • database. It provides specific information used to identify, c ategorize, and manage entities
  • effectively. Without attributes, entities have no meaningful data .(1)
  • Example –Single, Composite ,Multivalued etc. (1)

questions.question: Compare entity integrity and referential integrity constraints with examples. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare entity integrity and referential integrity constraints with examples.
  • [An][CO2]
  • Entity integrity ensures that every table has a unique and non-null primary key, so each
  • record can be uniquely identified. Referential integrity ensures that a foreign key in one
  • table matches a valid primary key value in another table, maintaining consistency
  • between related tables.
  • For example, in a STUDENT table, StudentID (Primary Key) cannot be null (entity
  • integrity), and in an ENROLLMENT table, StudentID (Foreign Key) must match a
  • valid StudentID in the STUDENT table (referential integrity).
  • Comparison and explanation – 5 marks

questions.question: Show How to draw an E-R diagram of a Library Database. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• E-R diagram of a Library Database [K]/[CO1]
  • The following may be used as a reference for this question.
  • A library database ER diagram may include entities like Book, Member
  • and Borrowing, connected by relationships. The Book entity has attributes like ISBN,
  • title, and author, while Member has Member ID and name. The Borrowing relationship
  • links a Member to a Book they have borrowed, often with attributes like the borrow
  • date and return date.
  • Entities and Attributes
  • • Book: Attributes include ISBN (Primary Key), title, author, and category.
  • • Member: Attributes include MemberID (Primary Key), name, address,
  • and phone number.
  • • Borrowing: This is a relationship entity that can have attributes
  • like borrow_date and return_date.
  • Relationships
  • • Member "borrows" Book: A member can borrow multiple books, and a book
  • can be borrowed by multiple members, making it a many-to-many relationship
  • (often resolved with the Borrowing entity).
  • • Borrowing links Member and Book: The Borrowing entity connects a specific
  • member to a specific book, recording the details of that borrowing event.
  • Example ER Diagram Structure
  • • Book (Entity)
  • o ISBN (Primary Key)
  • o title
  • o author
  • • Member (Entity)
  • o MemberID (Primary Key)
  • o name
  • • Borrowing (Relationship/Junction Entity)
  • o borrow_date
  • o return_date
  • o MemberID (Foreign Key referencing Member)
  • o ISBN (Foreign Key referencing Book)
  • This structure allows the database to track which member has borrowed which book
  • and when it is due to be returned.
  • Sample diagram with relevant entities, attributes and relationships (15 marks)

questions.question: Describe in detail the working of nested queries in SQL. Give suitable examples and write SQL queries that use nested queries in SELECT, WHERE, and HAVING clauses. / [CO3] [15x1 = 15]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe in detail the working of nested queries in SQL. Give suitable examples and
  • write SQL queries that use nested queries in SELECT, WHERE, and HA VING clauses
  • [S]/[CO3]
  • A nested query (or subquery) in SQL is a query inside another query that helps retrieve
  • data based on the results of the inner query. It can appear in the SELECT, WHERE, or
  • HA VING clause.
  • Example (SELECT):
  • SELECT Name, (SELECT DeptName FROM Department WHERE
  • Department.DeptID = Employee.DeptID) AS DepartmentName
  • FROM Employee;
  • Example (WHERE):
  • SELECT Name FROM Employee WHERE DeptID = (SELECT DeptID
  • FROM Department WHERE DeptName = 'HR');
  • Example (HA VING):
  • SELECT DeptID, A VG(Salary) FROM Employee
  • GROUP BY DeptID
  • HA VING A VG(Salary) > (SELECT A VG(Salary) FROM Employee);
  • [15 x 1 = 15]
